title: Job Scheduler
tagline: A job queue built from scratch: Redis sorted sets, retries with backoff, a dead-letter path, and a live dashboard fed by Redis pub/sub over WebSockets.
author: Chirag Mukhija

walkthrough.title: A job is submitted
walkthrough.body: POST /jobs checks the body (400 for a bad type, priority or delay), writes the job to Postgres as the durable record, adds its id to the Redis sorted set for its priority tier (scored by run time, so Redis can find what's due), publishes job:created, and answers 201 with the row. The Postgres write and the Redis write are separate steps: if Redis fails between them, the job exists but no worker will ever pick it up.

walkthrough.title: A worker claims work
walkthrough.body: The worker checks the 10 priority tiers in order, 0 first, and takes the earliest due job from the first tier that has one; when nothing is due, that's 10 Redis checks and no SQL. It claims the job with a guarded UPDATE (WHERE status = 'pending') so two workers can't both take it, removes it from Redis, and runs the handler for its type (send_email or resize_image, both stubs that only log). Then it marks the job completed, schedules a retry after 5 s, 10 s, 20 s and so on, or dead-letters it as 'failed' once its attempts run out.

walkthrough.title: How the dashboard stays live
walkthrough.body: Both the API (job:created) and the workers (claimed, completed, failed, and a heartbeat every 5 s) publish on the Redis channel job:events. The API listens on a dedicated Redis connection and pushes every event to each open WebSocket. The page updates its job table from the message itself, then calls GET /stats again for counts and worker status, for every message, heartbeats included. That refetch is what a scale finding flags.

walkthrough.title: The page also polls
walkthrough.body: On top of the live socket, the dashboard re-fetches /stats every 5 seconds. GET /stats counts jobs per status over the whole table and adds worker presence from the API's memory, where a worker heard from in the last 15 s counts as online.

walkthrough.title: Workers announce themselves
walkthrough.body: Every 5 seconds each worker publishes worker:heartbeat without waiting for it (a failure is only logged). The API's subscriber records the last-seen time in its own memory, which GET /stats reads; that record is lost whenever the API restarts.

title: InstaBackend
tagline: An Instagram-style API: JWT access tokens with refresh sessions in Redis, S3 presigned uploads, fan-out feeds and keyset pagination behind Nginx.
author: Chirag Mukhija

walkthrough.title: Signing up
walkthrough.body: Nginx checks its per-IP limit and forwards the request; five library middleware run, then the auth limiter counts the request in Redis (20 per 15 minutes per IP, shared by register, login and refresh). The service checks that the email and username are free, hashes the password with bcrypt at work factor 12 (about 260 ms on libuv's thread pool, which the request waits for), inserts the user, and stores a refresh-token session in Redis for 7 days.

walkthrough.title: Publishing a post fans it out
walkthrough.body: Creating a post also copies it into every follower's feed (fan-out on write): one query fetches all follower ids, then one INSERT with two parameters per follower. That's fine for most users, but Postgres allows at most 65,535 parameters per statement, so above about 32,000 followers the INSERT fails, after the post itself was already saved outside any transaction.

walkthrough.title: Reading the precomputed feed
walkthrough.body: This reads the feed_items rows written at post time, so a read is one indexed query. Compare it with GET /api/feed/fanout-read, which joins follows and posts on every read instead.

walkthrough.title: Uploads skip the API
walkthrough.body: The server signs an S3 upload URL locally, with no network call at all, and the browser sends the image straight to S3 with it. The server never contacts S3.

walkthrough.title: A profile is four queries
walkthrough.body: Loading a profile runs one lookup, then three COUNT queries in parallel with Promise.all, so it waits for the slowest of the three rather than all of them in a row.

title: Payment Gateway
tagline: Idempotent payments on Postgres: API-key auth on every /payments request, and each payment plus its first audit event in one transaction.
author: Chirag Mukhija

walkthrough.title: Creating a payment
walkthrough.body: Auth looks up the merchant by API key (401 if the header is missing or unknown) and the body is validated (400). If this merchant already used the idempotency key, the stored payment comes back with 201 and X-Idempotent-Replay: true, and nothing is written. Otherwise the payment and its first audit event are written in one transaction on one checked-out connection: BEGIN, two INSERTs, COMMIT (ROLLBACK on error), and the connection is released in finally. If two requests with the same key race past the check, the UNIQUE (merchant_id, idempotency_key) constraint makes the second INSERT fail, and that request gets 409.

walkthrough.title: Reading a payment
walkthrough.body: After the auth lookup, two queries: the payment by id, filtered to this merchant (another merchant's id gets 404), then its events. Today every payment has exactly one event, INITIATED.

walkthrough.title: Listing payments
walkthrough.body: LIMIT/OFFSET pagination: 20 rows by default, at most 100, newest first. The (merchant_id, created_at) index serves the order, but a deep offset still makes Postgres walk past every skipped row.

title: Hackathon Starter
tagline: A popular Express + MongoDB starter with Passport logins, sessions in MongoDB, email, and dozens of third-party API examples. A big real codebase to explore.
author: Sahat Yalkabov
license: MIT License; code excerpts shown under it

walkthrough.title: Signing up
walkthrough.body: Fifteen middleware run first. Among them, express-session loads the visitor's session from MongoDB (if the browser sent a cookie) and the CSRF check verifies the form token; Passport finds no logged-in user, so it skips the user lookup. The handler looks up the email. If it's taken, it emails a sign-in link to that account (a new SMTP connection per email). Otherwise it saves the new user, and a pre-save hook hashes the password with bcrypt first. The session is written back to MongoDB as the response ends.

walkthrough.title: Waiting on someone else's API
walkthrough.body: This page waits on the New York Times API with no timeout set; Node's fetch then waits about 5 minutes before giving up. The list changes weekly, so caching the response would remove the wait for almost every visitor.

walkthrough.title: Charging a card
walkthrough.body: The browser gets a one-time card token from Stripe, so card details never reach this server; the server sends that token to Stripe's Charges API and waits. Only a declined card is handled as an error: any other failure (a bad key, a network error) is shown to the user as a successful charge.

walkthrough.title: Changing a password
walkthrough.body: isAuthenticated guards the route. The handler loads the user again (req.user already holds it), sets the new password, and save() runs a pre-save hook that hashes it with bcrypt (work factor 10) before updating MongoDB.
